rules.rule: Authority substring extraction: after the literal "://" is found, let rest = input.substr(pos_of_scheme_sep + 3). The raw authority is rest.substr(0, rest.find_first_of("/?#")) — i.e. it ends at the FIRST occurrence of any of '/', '?', '#' (whichever comes first), or end-of-string. Everything from that delimiter onward is the path/query/fragment part. Verified: "http://u/p@h" -> authority "u", path "/p@h"; "http://a?b@c" -> authority "a", query "b@c"; "http://a#b@c" -> authority "a", fragment "b@c".

Userinfo split: inside the raw authority, find the FIRST '@' (find('@'), not rfind). userinfo = authority_raw.substr(0, first_at); host_port = authority_raw.substr(first_at+1). If there is no '@', userinfo = "" and host_port = whole raw authority. Verified: "http://a@b@c.com" -> userinfo "a", host "b@c.com"; "http://a@b@c@d.com" -> userinfo "a", host "b@c@d.com"; "http://a@@@b" -> userinfo "a", host "@@b"; "http://@a@b" -> userinfo "", host "a@b".

All '@' characters after the first one are kept verbatim in host(): they are NOT stripped and do NOT re-trigger a split. "http://a@@b" -> host "@b"; "http://u@h@" -> host "h@"; "http://@@@" -> userinfo "", host "@@"; "http://u@@:80" -> host "@", port 80.

host/port split happens on host_port AFTER the userinfo split, at the FIRST ':' in host_port: host = host_port.substr(0, first_colon), port_str = host_port.substr(first_colon+1) parsed stoi-style (leading digits, rest ignored; invalid/out-of-range => absent). Evidence for FIRST (not last) ':': "http://h:80:90" -> host "h", port 80; "http://u@[::1]:80" -> host "[", port absent (port_str "::1]:80" fails stoi); "http://u@h:@80" -> host "h", port absent (port_str "@80").

Because port parsing is stoi-prefix based, any '@' that follows a numeric port inside the authority is silently swallowed and lost: "http://a@b:80@c" -> userinfo "a", host "b", port 80, path/query/fragment all empty, to_string "http://a@b:80" (the "@c" vanishes). Same for "http://u@h:80@" -> to_string "http://u@h:80".

Empty userinfo (authority begins with '@'): userinfo = "" and has_userinfo = 0; the '@' is dropped from the reconstructed authority() and to_string(). "http://@example.com" -> authority "example.com", userinfo "", has_userinfo 0, to_string "http://example.com"; "http://@b.com:80/p" -> to_string "http://b.com:80/p".

Userinfo present with empty host: userinfo is kept, host is "", has_host 0, has_authority 0, but authority() still renders the trailing '@'. "http://user@" -> authority "user@", userinfo "user", host "", has_authority 0, is_valid 0. "http://user@:8080" -> authority "user@:8080", port 8080, has_authority 0, is_valid 0.

authority() is reconstructed as: (userinfo.empty() ? "" : userinfo + "@") + host + (port != -1 ? ":" + to_string(port) : ""). Verified across: "http://u@:80/p" -> "u@:80"; "http://:@:80" -> ":@:80"; "http://a@" -> "a@"; "http://@:80" -> ":80"; "http://u@h:" -> "u@h" (trailing colon dropped); "http://a@b://c" -> authority "a@b" (raw was "a@b:") and to_string "http://a@b//c".

userinfo keeps ':' characters entirely — there is no user/password split. "http://u:p@h" -> userinfo "u:p"; "http://u:p:q@h" -> userinfo "u:p:q"; "http://:@h" -> userinfo ":" (has_userinfo 1); "http://u:@h" -> userinfo "u:"; "http://:p@h" -> userinfo ":p". The ':' inside userinfo never affects port parsing ("http://h:80@u" -> userinfo "h:80", host "u", port -1).

userinfo is byte-for-byte verbatim: no percent-decoding, no case folding, no whitespace trimming, no length limit. "http://U%7Eser@h" -> userinfo "U%7Eser"; "http://a%40b@h" -> "a%40b" (does NOT decode to '@' and does not re-split); "http://%75@h" -> "%75"; "http://ABC@h" -> "ABC"; "HTTP://U@H.COM" -> scheme "http" but userinfo "U", host "H.COM"; "http:// @h" -> userinfo " " (has_userinfo 1); "http://a b@h" -> "a b"; tab and newline inside userinfo are preserved (verified via od -c); "http://ü@h" -> userinfo "ü"; 300-char userinfo preserved at length 300.

An '@' that lies after the authority terminator is NEVER userinfo — it stays in path/query/fragment. "http://example.com/a@b" -> path "/a@b"; "http://example.com?x=a@b" -> query "x=a@b"; "http://example.com#a@b" -> fragment "a@b"; "http://u@h:80/p@q" -> userinfo "u", host "h", port 80, path "/p@q"; "http://u@h?a@b#c@d" -> query "a@b", fragment "c@d"; "http://a/b@c:80" -> path "/b@c:80" and port stays absent.
has_userinfo() == !userinfo.empty(). Confirmed by userinfo ":" -> 1, " " -> 1, "" (leading '@') -> 0.

has_authority() == !host.empty() (equivalently has_host()). Userinfo and port do not make has_authority true. "http://user@:8080" -> authority ":"-bearing string, has_port 1, has_authority 0; "http://:@:80" -> has_authority 0; "http://@@" -> host "@" -> has_authority 1.

is_valid() == (!host.empty() || !path.empty()); userinfo, port, query and fragment are irrelevant. Evidence: "http://a@" -> 0; "http://a@/p" -> 1 (path only); "http://a@:/p" -> 1; "http://u@/" -> 1; "http://a@?q" -> 0; "http://a@#f" -> 0; "http://u@?@" -> 0; "http://u@:0" -> 0 (port set, still 0); "http://u@:80/p" -> 1; "http:///p" -> 1; "?q" -> 0; "#f" -> 0; "http://@@" -> 1 (host "@").

Degenerate all-'@' cases: "http://@" -> userinfo "", host "", authority "", to_string "http://", is_valid 0. "http://@@" -> userinfo "", host "@", to_string "http://@", is_valid 1. "http://@:80" -> userinfo "", host "", port 80, authority ":80", has_authority 0, is_valid 0. "http://@:@h" -> userinfo "", host "" (host_port ":@h" -> first ':' -> host "", port "@h" invalid), authority "", to_string "http://", is_valid 0. "http://u@:@h" -> userinfo "u", host "", port -1, authority "u@", is_valid 0.

No IPv6 bracket awareness anywhere in authority parsing: brackets are ordinary characters, so a bracketed literal before '@' becomes userinfo and one after '@' gets chopped at its first ':'. "http://[::1]@h" -> userinfo "[::1]", host "h"; "http://u@[::1]:80" -> userinfo "u", host "[", port -1, authority "u@[", to_string "http://u@[" (rest of the address is silently discarded).

Userinfo parsing is scheme-independent (http, https, ftp, and even the odd scheme "u@http" behave identically). "https://u@h" -> userinfo "u"; "ftp://u:p@h:21/x" -> userinfo "u:p", host "h", port 21, path "/x"; "u@http://h" -> scheme "u@http", authority "h", userinfo "" (the '@' before "://" belongs to the scheme, not userinfo).

Pseudocode for the whole userinfo/host/port stage: sep = input.find("://"); if none -> no authority at all. scheme = lowercase(input[0..sep)); rest = input[sep+3..]; e = rest.find_first_of("/?#"); auth_raw = rest[0..e); remainder = rest[e..]. at = auth_raw.find('@'); if at != npos { userinfo = auth_raw[0..at); hp = auth_raw[at+1..]; } else { userinfo = ""; hp = auth_raw; } c = hp.find(':'); if c != npos { host = hp[0..c); port = stoi_prefix(hp[c+1..]) with 0<=p<=65535 else -1; } else { host = hp; port = -1; }. Then remainder is split by first '#' then first '?'.

rules.rule: MAJOR / ORDERING: the fragment and query are stripped from the ENTIRE raw input BEFORE scheme detection, not after authority parsing. Algorithm: s = argv[1]; i = s.find('#'); if (i != npos) { fragment = s.substr(i+1); s = s.substr(0,i); } j = s.find('?'); if (j != npos) { query = s.substr(j+1); s = s.substr(0,j); } then parse scheme/authority/path from the shortened s. Proof: "http#://ex.com" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, path "http", fragment "://ex.com". The literal "://" is present in the raw input, yet no scheme is found, because it was already moved into the fragment. Same for "ht?tp://ex.com/p" -> path "ht", query "tp://ex.com/p", no scheme.

'#' is located first (over the whole input) and '?' is searched only in the prefix before that '#'. Consequences that hold universally: query() can NEVER contain '#'; fragment() CAN contain both '#' and '?'; path() can contain NEITHER '?' nor '#'. Evidence: "a/b#c?d" -> path "a/b", query "" (has_query 0), fragment "c?d"; "http://ex.com/a?b?c#d#e" -> path "/a", query "b?c", fragment "d#e".

Only the FIRST '#' is a delimiter; every later '#' stays verbatim in the fragment. Only the FIRST '?' in the pre-'#' prefix is a delimiter; every later '?' stays verbatim in the query. Evidence: "a#b#c" -> fragment "b#c"; "a?b?c" -> query "b?c"; "http://ex.com/##" -> fragment "#"; "http://ex.com/??" -> query "?".

Because '?' and '#' are already removed before scheme/authority parsing, the authority region ends at the FIRST '/' in the post-"://" remainder ONLY. The apparent rule "authority ends at first of '/', '?', '#'" is an observational consequence, not a separate check. Implement as: rest = s.substr(pos_of_"://" + 3); k = rest.find('/'); authority_region = (k==npos ? rest : rest.substr(0,k)); path = (k==npos ? "" : rest.substr(k)). Evidence: "http://ex.com?x:80" -> host "ex.com", port -1, query "x:80"; "http://ex#.com/p" -> host "ex", fragment ".com/p"; "http://ex.com:8#0/p" -> host "ex.com", port 8, fragment "0/p".

When a scheme was found ("://" present in the post-strip string), path() is either the empty string (no '/' in the remainder) or a string that ALWAYS begins with '/'. A non-slash-prefixed path after an authority is impossible. Evidence: "http://ex.com" -> path "", has_path 0; "http://ex.com/" -> path "/", has_path 1; "http://ex.com?x" -> path "".

Backslash is NOT a delimiter and does not terminate the authority: "http://ex.com\\p" (one literal backslash) -> host "ex.com\p", authority "ex.com\p", path "", has_path 0, is_valid 1. Only '/' (and the pre-stripped '?'/'#') end the authority region.

The path is taken from the first '/' INCLUSIVE, so extra slashes are preserved and empty authority is possible: "http:///p" -> authority "", has_authority 0, host "", path "/p"; "http:////p" -> authority "", path "//p"; "http://ex.com//a//b" -> path "//a//b".

With NO scheme (no "://" after the '#'/'?' strip), the whole remaining string becomes path() verbatim, including leading slashes; no authority is parsed. Evidence: "/" -> path "/"; "//" -> path "//" (host "", has_authority 0); "a" -> path "a"; "ex.com?q=1" -> path "ex.com", query "q=1"; "/a/./b/../c?x=./y#z/../w" -> path "/a/./b/../c", query "x=./y", fragment "z/../w".

Query/fragment splitting applies EQUALLY to scheme-less input — there is no requirement of a scheme or authority. Evidence: "a/b?c#d" -> path "a/b", query "c", fragment "d"; "?q=1" -> path "", query "q=1"; "#f" -> fragment "f".

An empty piece after a delimiter yields an empty string with the corresponding has_*() == 0, and the delimiter is DROPPED from to_string() (lossy round-trip). Evidence: "http://ex.com/?" -> query "", has_query 0, to_string "http://ex.com/"; "http://ex.com/#" -> fragment "", has_fragment 0, to_string "http://ex.com/"; "http://ex.com/?#" -> both empty, to_string "http://ex.com/"; "?" -> to_string ""; "#" -> to_string "".

has_query() == !query.empty() and has_fragment() == !fragment.empty() and has_path() == !path.empty(). There is no separate "delimiter was present" flag. Evidence: "http://ex.com?#" -> has_query 0, has_fragment 0, identical output to "http://ex.com" except nothing; "http://ex.com/##" -> fragment "#" so has_fragment 1.

path()/query()/fragment() are byte-verbatim substrings: no percent-decoding, no normalization, no case folding, no whitespace trimming. '&', '=', '+', ';', '%', ':', '@', spaces, and tabs all survive. Evidence: "http://ex.com/?a=1&b=2;c+d=e%20f" -> query "a=1&b=2;c+d=e%20f"; "http://ex.com/#a=1&b;c+d%7E" -> fragment "a=1&b;c+d%7E"; "http://ex.com/p;a=1&b=2+c=%7E" -> path "/p;a=1&b=2+c=%7E"; "HTTP://EX.COM/PaTh?Q=A#F" -> path "/PaTh", query "Q=A", fragment "F" (case preserved; only scheme lowercased); "http://ex.com/ ?  # " -> path "/ ", query "  ", fragment " "; "   " -> path "   ", is_valid 1; tab-containing input verified byte-exact via od -c.

'://' at offset 0 produces an EMPTY scheme with has_scheme 0, yet the authority IS still parsed (because a "://" was found). Evidence: "://ex.com" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, authority "ex.com", has_authority 1, host "ex.com", to_string "" ; "://u@ex.com:80/p?q#f" -> userinfo "u", host "ex.com", port 80, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", has_scheme 0, to_string "/p?q#f".

to_string() reconstruction: out = ""; if (has_scheme()) out += scheme + "://" + authority(); if (has_path()) out += path; if (has_query()) out += "?" + query; if (has_fragment()) out += "#" + fragment. Note the authority is emitted ONLY inside the has_scheme branch, so a parsed authority with an empty scheme is silently lost. Evidence: "://ex.com" -> to_string "" despite authority "ex.com"; "://ex.com/p" -> to_string "/p"; "http:///p" -> to_string "http:///p" (scheme + "://" + "" + "/p"); "a://b://c/p" -> to_string "a://b//c/p" (authority region "b:" reconstructed as "b", port dropped).

to_string() is lossy in exactly three ways relevant to this family: (a) an empty query/fragment loses its '?'/'#' delimiter, (b) an authority with no scheme is dropped entirely, (c) an unparseable/empty port loses its ':'. Evidence for (a)+(b) combined: "http://ex.com/?#?#" -> path "/", query "", fragment "?#", to_string "http://ex.com/#?#" (the '?' of the empty query is gone).

is_valid() == has_host() || has_path()  (equivalently: !host.empty() || !path.empty()). Scheme, query and fragment do NOT contribute. Evidence for 1: "/" (path only) -> 1; "a" -> 1; "://ex.com" (host, no scheme, no path) -> 1; "http#://ex.com" (path "http" only) -> 1; "   " -> 1. Evidence for 0: "?q=1" -> 0; "#f" -> 0; "?" -> 0; "#" -> 0; "?#" -> 0; "#?" -> 0; "#/" -> 0 (fragment "/" only); "?/" -> 0; "http://#ex.com" -> has_scheme 1 but host "" and path "" -> 0; "a://" -> 0; "://" -> 0.

has_authority() == has_host() == !host.empty() in every probe run; the reconstructed authority string being non-empty is irrelevant. Evidence: "http:///p" -> authority "", has_authority 0; "://ex.com" -> has_authority 1; "http://ex.com:8#0/p" -> authority "ex.com:8", host "ex.com", has_authority 1; combined with the given fact "http://:8080" -> authority ":8080" but has_authority 0.

ambiguities: SURPRISING (but firmly established): the '#'/'?' split runs over the RAW input before the "://" scheme search. This means a '#' or '?' occurring anywhere before the "://" destroys scheme AND authority parsing entirely ("http#://ex.com" has no scheme and no host). Any reimplementation that parses the scheme first and only then splits query/fragment will diverge on these inputs. This is the single highest-risk rule in this family.

SURPRISING: to_string() emits the authority only when has_scheme() is true, so "://ex.com" round-trips to the empty string even though host()/authority() are populated and is_valid() is 1. I could not find any input with an empty scheme whose to_string included the authority.

to_string() is not injective: "http://ex.com", "http://ex.com?", "http://ex.com#", and "http://ex.com?#" all produce to_string "http://ex.com". Likewise "http://ex.com/?#?#" -> "http://ex.com/#?#". So an empty-but-present query/fragment is unrecoverable.

Marked 'likely' rather than 'certain' only because the rule is inferred from coincidence across cases rather than from an isolating probe.

has_authority() tracked has_host() exactly in all probes; I never found an input where they differed. It is possible the implementation checks something subtly different (e.g. "host non-empty" vs "authority region contained a host"), but no probe distinguishes them.

I did not test bytes above 0x7F (UTF-8 / raw high bytes) or embedded NUL in the path/query/fragment; NUL cannot be passed through argv at all, and multi-byte behavior is presumed byte-verbatim by analogy with tabs and spaces but was not directly probed.
Very long inputs (length-based truncation or overflow in the splitting code) were not probed.

result.family: HOST / PORT SPLITTING inside the authority (authority reconstruction, has_authority/has_host, IPv6, empty-host cases)

rules.rule: Authority extent: after the literal "://", the raw authority substring runs from just past "://" up to (exclusive) the FIRST occurrence of any of '/', '?', '#' (whichever comes first); if none occur, the authority is the whole remainder. Everything from that delimiter onward is handled by the path/query/fragment stage. Consequence: the authority can never contain '/', '?' or '#'. Evidence: "http://host/p:80" -> host "host", port -1, path "/p:80"; "http://host?q:80" -> host "host", port -1, query "q:80"; "http://host#f:80" -> host "host", port -1, fragment "f:80"; "http://a#b:80/c" -> host "a", fragment "b:80/c".

Inside the raw authority, userinfo is split off at the FIRST '@': userinfo = text before the first '@', hostport = everything after it (which may itself contain further '@' characters, all of which become part of the host). If there is no '@', userinfo is empty and hostport = whole authority. Evidence: "http://u@h@host:80" -> userinfo "u", host "h@host", port 80; "http://a@b@c:1" -> userinfo "a", host "b@c", port 1.

Host/port split uses the FIRST ':' in the hostport part, NOT the last. host = text before that first ':'; the port candidate string = everything after that first ':' (up to the end of the authority), including any further ':' characters. Evidence: "http://a:80:90" -> host "a", port 80 (candidate "80:90"); "http://a:1:2" -> host "a", port 1 (candidate "1:2"); "http://a:b:c" -> host "a", port -1 (candidate "b:c" fails to parse); "http://a::80" -> host "a", port -1 (candidate ":80" fails); "http://a:::" -> host "a", port -1.

The port candidate string is parsed like std::stoi with a subsequent range check 0 <= port <= 65535: leading whitespace and a leading '+' are skipped, leading zeros are ignored, parsing stops at the first non-digit and the digits seen so far are used, and a candidate with no leading digits (after optional sign/whitespace) yields NO port (-1). Out-of-range values yield NO port. Evidence: "http://host:080" -> 80; "http://a:0080" -> 80; "http://host:+80" -> 80; "http://host: 80" -> 80; "http://host:8 0" -> 8; "http://host:80abc/p" -> port 80, path "/p"; "http://host:65535" -> 65535; "http://host:65536" -> -1; "http://host:2147483647" -> -1; "http://host:2147483648" -> -1; "http://host:-1" -> -1; "http://host: " -> -1; "http://host::" -> -1; "http://a:b:c" -> -1.

There is NO IPv6 / bracket special-casing whatsoever. A bracketed IPv6 literal is mangled by the naive first-':' split: the host becomes only the text up to the first ':' (so it keeps the opening '[' but loses the rest), and the port candidate becomes the remainder of the address, which never parses. Evidence: "http://[::1]/" -> host "[", port -1, path "/", authority "[", to_string "http://[/"; "http://[::1]:8080/" -> identical output (host "[", port -1, path "/") — the :8080 is silently lost; "http://[2001:db8::1]:80/p" -> host "[2001", port -1, path "/p", to_string "http://[2001/p"; "http://[::ffff:1.2.3.4]:80" -> host "[", port -1; "http://[::1]:x" -> host "[", port -1.

Brackets are ordinary characters, so a bracketed string with NO internal ':' keeps its brackets in the host and the port after ']' IS found (because ':' after ']' is simply the first ':'). Evidence: "http://[]:80" -> host "[]", port 80, authority "[]:80", to_string "http://[]:80"; "http://[v1.x]:80" -> host "[v1.x]", port 80, authority "[v1.x]:80"; "http://[]" -> host "[]", port -1; "http://a]:80" -> host "a]", port 80.

authority() is RECONSTRUCTED, never the raw substring, as: (userinfo.empty() ? "" : userinfo + "@") + host + (port == -1 ? "" : ":" + to_string(port)). No brackets are ever added around host; host is emitted verbatim (possibly empty). Evidence: "http://u@host:80" -> "u@host:80"; "http://@host" -> "host" (the empty userinfo's '@' is dropped); "http://u@" -> "u@"; "http://u@:80" -> "u@:80"; "http://:8080" -> ":8080"; "http://:" -> ""; "http://a:80:90" -> "a:80"; "http://a:b:c" -> "a"; "http://host:080" -> "host:80"; "http://:@:80" -> ":@:80" (userinfo ":" is non-empty so '@' kept).

has_host() == !host.empty() — a raw byte-level emptiness test, with no trimming. A host of a single space counts as present. Evidence: "http:// :80" -> host " ", has_host 1, authority " :80"; "http://:8080" -> host "", has_host 0; "http://[::1]/" -> host "[", has_host 1.

has_authority() == has_host() == !host.empty(). It is NOT "authority string non-empty": whenever host is empty, has_authority is 0 even though authority() renders non-empty text from userinfo and/or port. No probe produced has_authority != has_host. Evidence: "http://:8080" -> authority ":8080", has_authority 0; "http://u@" -> authority "u@", has_authority 0; "http://u@:80" -> authority "u@:80", has_authority 0; "http://:@:80" -> authority ":@:80", has_authority 0; "http://[]:80" -> authority "[]:80", has_authority 1; "http:// :80" -> has_authority 1.

An empty host does NOT suppress the port: port is parsed and reported independently of whether host is empty, and it still appears in authority() and to_string(). Evidence: "http://:8080" -> host "", port 8080, has_port 1, to_string "http://:8080"; "http://:0" -> port 0, has_port 1; "http://@:80" -> userinfo "", host "", port 80, authority ":80"; "http://:80:90" -> host "", port 80, authority ":80".

An authority consisting only of ":" (or only of "@") collapses to all-empty: host "", userinfo "", port -1, so authority() and to_string() render as if the authority were absent. Evidence: "http://:" -> authority "", to_string "http://"; "http://@" -> authority "", to_string "http://"; "http://:/path" -> authority "", path "/path", to_string "http:///path" (the ":" is lost, so to_string is NOT byte-identical to the input).

host() is never normalized: case is preserved exactly, trailing dots are kept, underscores/hyphens/digits/backslashes/brackets/spaces/tabs are kept, percent escapes are NOT decoded, and non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes pass through unchanged (no IDNA/punycode, no lowercasing of non-ASCII). Only scheme() is lowercased. Evidence: "http://EXAMPLE.COM:80/P" -> host "EXAMPLE.COM", path "/P", scheme "http"; "HTTP://HOST:80" -> scheme "http", host "HOST"; "http://example.com./p" -> host "example.com."; "http://ex_am-ple9.com:80" -> host "ex_am-ple9.com"; "http://ex%41mple.com" -> host "ex%41mple.com"; "http://a%3A80" -> host "a%3A80", port -1 (escaped colon is not a delimiter); "http://exämple.com:80/ä" -> host bytes ex\303\244mple.com verbatim (od-verified); "http://Ω:80" -> host "Ω", port 80; "http://a\\b" -> host "a\\b"; "http://ho st:80" -> host "ho st"; "http://host :80" -> host "host " (trailing space kept), port 80.

Because the '@' split precedes the ':' split, a ':' that lies before the first '@' belongs to userinfo and produces no port; conversely a host-looking prefix before ':' can end up as userinfo. Evidence: "http://u:80@host" -> userinfo "u:80", host "host", port -1; "http://host:80@u" -> userinfo "host:80", host "u", port -1; "http://a:b@c:d" -> userinfo "a:b", host "c", port -1; "http://host:8@0" -> userinfo "host:8", host "0", port -1.

Because the authority ends at the first '/', '?' or '#', a '#' or '?' before any ':' prevents port parsing entirely, and the '@' after such a delimiter is not a userinfo delimiter. Evidence: "http://a:b#c@d" -> authority "a", host "a", userinfo "", port -1, fragment "c@d", to_string "http://a#c@d"; "http://a#b#c" -> host "a", fragment "b#c"; "http://a?b/c" -> host "a", query "b/c", path "".

to_string() == (has_scheme ? scheme + "://" : "") + authority() + path + (query.empty() ? "" : "?" + query) + (fragment.empty() ? "" : "#" + fragment). The "://" is emitted whenever a scheme exists, even when the authority is empty (yielding "http:///path" or bare "http://"). Evidence: "http:///path" -> "http:///path"; "http://" -> "http://"; "http://:80/" -> "http://:80/"; "http://a:b:c/p?q#f" -> "http://a/p?q#f"; "http://[::1]/p?q#f" -> "http://[/p?q#f"; "http://a:80?q=1:2#f:3" -> "http://a:80?q=1:2#f:3"; "//host/p" (no scheme) -> "//host/p".

is_valid() == (!host.empty() || !path.empty()), i.e. has_host() || has_path(). Port, query, fragment, userinfo and scheme presence do not contribute. Evidence: "http://:8080" -> 0; "http://?q" -> 0; "http://#f" -> 0; "http://:8080?q" -> 0 (port+query but no host/path); "http://u@" -> 0; "http://:@:80" -> 0; "http:///path" -> 1; "http://:8080/p" -> 1; "http://u@/p" -> 1 (empty host but path present); "http://:80/" -> 1; "?q" -> 0; "#f" -> 0; ":8080" -> 1 (whole thing is path); "http://[" family e.g. "http://[::1]" -> 1 (host "[" non-empty).

has_userinfo() == !userinfo.empty(); a userinfo of just ":" counts as present. Evidence: "http://@host" -> userinfo "", has_userinfo 0, authority "host"; "http://:@host" -> userinfo ":", has_userinfo 1, authority ":@host".

When the authority is empty/absent (no host, no port, no userinfo) but a path follows, the path retains its leading '/' and to_string re-emits "://" + "" + path. There is no synthesis of a host from the path's first segment. Evidence: "http:///path" -> authority "", path "/path", has_authority 0, is_valid 1; "//host/p" (no "://") -> no scheme, path "//host/p", has_host 0.

ambiguities: Cannot distinguish two implementations that are behaviorally identical here: (a) the authority substring is cut at the first of '/','?','#' and then fragment/query are split from the remainder, versus (b) the fragment is split at the first '#' and the query at the first '?' globally, and only then is the authority cut at the first '/'. Every probe I tried ("http://a#b:80/c", "http://a#b#c", "http://a?b/c", "http://a:b#c@d", "http://host?q:80") gives the same output under both models. Implement either; I found no discriminating input.

has_authority() is indistinguishable from has_host() in all 104 probes. It could be implemented as !host.empty(), or as a separate flag that happens to coincide. If the real implementation stores a distinct 'authority present' flag, no probe I ran exposes a difference — including cases where authority() renders non-empty text ("u@", ":8080", ":@:80") while has_authority is 0.

Whether the port range check is exactly [0,65535] or is 'parse as int then reject if <0 or >65535' cannot be fully separated: "http://host:65536" and "http://host:2147483648" both give -1, so an overflow-throw and a range-reject are indistinguishable at 2147483648. 65535 accepted / 65536 rejected pins the upper bound; "-1" rejected pins the lower bound at >= 0 (0 is accepted).

Round-trip is lossy in ways that may be surprising: to_string() is NOT byte-identical to the input whenever the port candidate had extra text ("http://a:80:90" -> "http://a:80"), had leading zeros ("http://host:080" -> "http://host:80"), was unparseable ("http://[::1]:8080/" -> "http://[/"), or when the authority contained a bare ':' or '@' ("http://:/path" -> "http:///path", "http://@host" -> "http://host"). I could not determine whether this is intentional normalization or just a side effect of reconstruction.

"http://[::1]:8080/" and "http://[::1]/" produce byte-identical 18-line output, so IPv6 URLs with and without a port are indistinguishable through this API. Any downstream consumer cannot recover the port. Flagging as almost certainly a bug in the library rather than a deliberate rule, but it must be replicated for byte-equality.

result.family: PORT NUMERIC PARSING (host:port split + std::stoi-style parse + range predicate)

rules.rule: Port text extraction: after the authority has been isolated (authority = text after "://" up to the first '/', '?' or '#'), and after userinfo is split off at '@', the remaining host_part is split at the FIRST ':' . host = text before it, port_text = ENTIRE remainder after it (may itself contain ':', '@' is impossible here since userinfo split already happened). Evidence: "http://h:12:34:56" -> host "h", port 12; "http://h:80:90" -> host "h", port 80; "http://h::" -> host "h", port absent (port_text ":" is unparsable). Not the last ':': last-colon splitting would have given host "h:12:34" / "h:".

Numeric parse is exactly std::stoi(port_text) wrapped in try/catch (base 10, no endptr check): (1) skip leading C-locale whitespace, (2) accept one optional '+' or '-', (3) consume the maximal run of ASCII digits, (4) STOP at the first non-digit and IGNORE the rest (no requirement that the whole string be digits). Evidence: "80abc"->80, "8a0"->8, "80 "->80, "6553 5"->6553, "0x10"->0, "0b1"->0, "1e3"->1, "6e4"->6, "1.5"->1, "80.9"->80, "6553.6"->6553, "1,000"->1, "65,536"->65, "65535abc"->65535, "80%20"->80, "80٣"->80, "80:"->80.

Leading whitespace IS skipped, and it is C-locale isspace: space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return all work, and multiple/mixed whitespace works. Evidence: "http://h: 80"->80, "http://h:\t80"->80, "http://h:\n80"->80, "http://h:\v80"->80, "http://h:\f80"->80, "http://h:\r80"->80, "http://h:  80"->80, "http://h: \t\n 80"->80. U+00A0 NBSP (bytes C2 A0) is NOT whitespace: "http://h:\xc2\xa080" -> port absent.

A single leading sign is accepted; whitespace may precede the sign but NOT follow it, and only one sign is allowed. Evidence: "+80"->80, "+00080"->80, "+65535"->65535, " +80"->80; but "+ 80"->absent, "- 80"->absent, " -80"->absent(negative), "++80"->absent, "--80"->absent, "+-80"->absent, bare "+"->absent, bare "-"->absent.

Accept/reject predicate on the parsed value: accept iff 0 <= value <= 65535 inclusive (65535 is valid, 0 is valid, so the range is 0..65535, NOT 1..65535). Evidence: "0"->0 accepted (has_port 1, to_string "http://h:0"), "1"->1, "65534"->65534, "65535"->65535 accepted; "65536","65537","70000","99999","655350","65535000","65536abc","2147483646" -> all absent.

Negative parsed values are rejected, but the sign is applied BEFORE the range check, so "-0" is accepted as 0. Evidence: "http://h:-0" -> port 0, has_port 1, authority "h:0", to_string "http://h:0"; "http://h:-1", "http://h:-80", "http://h:-65535", "http://h:-2147483648", "http://h:-2147483649" -> all port -1 / has_port 0.

Unparsable (zero digits consumed) => absent. This covers empty, whitespace-only, sign-only, and any string whose first non-space/non-sign char is not an ASCII digit. Evidence: "http://h:"->absent, "http://h::"->absent, "http://h: "->absent, "http://h:abc"->absent, "http://h:abc80"->absent, "http://h:abc:80"->absent, "http://h:.80"->absent, "http://h:_80"->absent, "http://h:%2080"->absent.

Only ASCII '0'-'9' count as digits — non-ASCII digit forms are rejected (no Unicode digit handling, no locale digit handling). Evidence: "http://h:٣" (U+0663 Arabic-Indic three) -> absent; "http://h:٣80" -> absent (stops immediately); "http://h:１２３" (fullwidth) -> absent; but "http://h:80٣" -> 80 (ASCII digits first, trailing garbage ignored).

Overflow beyond int range behaves as std::stoi's out_of_range => absent (indistinguishable from, and equivalent to, the >65535 rejection). Evidence: "2147483647"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "4294967296"->absent, "18446744073709551617"->absent, "99999999999999999999"->absent, "21474836470"->absent, "80000000000000000000000"->absent, 1000 '9' chars -> absent. Implementation note: you can implement this as a single check 0<=value<=65535 using arbitrary/64-bit precision — any value that would overflow int also exceeds 65535, so the observable behavior is identical.

Leading zeros are decimal, not octal, and do not cause overflow no matter how many there are. Evidence: "007"->7, "065"->65, "0080"->80, "00"->0, "0000"->0, "0777"->777 (not 511), "000000000000065535"->65535, "000000000000065536"->absent, 1000 zeros followed by "80"->80, 1000 zeros alone ->0, "000000000002147483648"->absent.

On rejection the ':' and the entire port text are DROPPED ENTIRELY: host keeps only the text before the ':', and the rejected text never appears in host(), path(), query(), fragment(), authority(), or to_string(). Evidence: "http://h:abc" -> host "h", path "", authority "h", to_string "http://h"; "http://h:65536" -> authority "h", to_string "http://h"; "http://h:80000000000000000000000" -> to_string "http://h".

A rejected/absent port has NO effect on is_valid(): is_valid stays 1 as long as the rest of the URL is valid. Evidence: "http://h:abc" -> is_valid 1; "http://h:65536" -> 1; "http://h:" -> 1; "http://h:-1" -> 1; "http://h:2147483648/p?q#f" -> 1. Conversely a VALID port does not rescue an empty host: "http://:80" -> port 80, has_port 1, authority ":80", to_string "http://:80", is_valid 0.

Path/query/fragment parsing is unaffected by port rejection — the authority terminator scan happens before port parsing. Evidence: "http://h:abc/p?q#f" -> host "h", port -1, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", to_string "http://h/p?q#f"; "http://h:65536/p?q#f" -> same shape; "http://h:2147483648/p?q#f" -> same; "http://h:80abc/p?q#f" -> port 80, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", to_string "http://h:80/p?q#f".

The port text never extends past the authority terminator, so '/', '?' and '#' effectively terminate the port digits (in addition to stoi stopping there anyway). Evidence: "http://h:8?0" -> port 8, query "0" (NOT port 80); "http://h:8#0" -> port 8, fragment "0"; "http://h:80?q=1" -> port 80 + query "q=1"; "http://h:80#f" -> port 80 + fragment "f"; "http://h:80/" -> port 80, path "/"; "http://h:0/" -> port 0, path "/".

A ':' that appears after the authority ends is never a port: it is ordinary path/query/fragment text. Evidence: "http://h/x:80" -> port -1, path "/x:80"; "http://h?x:80" -> query "x:80"; "http://h#x:80" -> fragment "x:80". And with no "://" there is no port at all: "example.com:8080" -> path "example.com:8080", port -1; "//h:8080" -> path "//h:8080", port -1.

Userinfo is split off BEFORE the host:port split, so a ':' inside userinfo is not a port and a ':' after '@' is. Evidence: "http://u:p@h:80" -> userinfo "u:p", host "h", port 80; "http://u:80@h" -> userinfo "u:80", host "h", port -1; "http://h:80@x" -> userinfo "h:80", host "x", port -1; "http://@h:80" -> userinfo "", host "h", port 80, authority "h:80"; "http://u:p@h:65536/x" -> userinfo "u:p", host "h", port -1, path "/x", to_string "http://u:p@h/x".

There is NO IPv6 bracket handling: the first ':' inside '[...]' is treated as the port delimiter, mangling the host. Evidence: "http://[::1]:8080" -> host "[", port -1 (port_text ":1]:8080" is unparsable), authority "[", to_string "http://[", is_valid 1.

No default-port suppression and no scheme-specific port logic: an accepted port is always echoed in authority() and to_string(), including 0 and scheme-default ports. Evidence: "http://h:80" -> to_string "http://h:80"; "https://h:443" -> "https://h:443"; "ftp://h:21" -> "ftp://h:21"; "http://h:0" -> "http://h:0". Port is printed canonically (re-serialized from the int), so leading zeros/sign/whitespace/trailing junk are normalized away: "http://h:+00080" -> to_string "http://h:80".

has_port() == (port() != -1), equivalently (port() >= 0). Since -1 can never be produced by a successful parse (negatives are rejected), the two formulations are behaviorally identical. Absent port prints exactly "-1" on line 5 with has_port 0.

Exact pseudocode for the predicate:
  parse_port(port_text) -> optional<int>:
    i = 0
    while i < len && isspace_c(port_text[i]): i++          // " \t\n\v\f\r"
    neg = false
    if i < len and (port_text[i]=='+' or port_text[i]=='-'):
        neg = (port_text[i]=='-'); i++
    start = i
    while i < len and '0' <= port_text[i] <= '9': i++
    if i == start: return NONE                              // stoi -> invalid_argument
    mag = decimal_value(port_text[start..i))                 // arbitrary precision
    if mag > 2147483647: return NONE                         // stoi -> out_of_range
    v = neg ? -mag : mag
    if v < 0 or v > 65535: return NONE                       // range check
    return v
  // NONE => port = -1, has_port = false, ':'+text omitted from authority() and to_string(); is_valid() unaffected.

ambiguities: std::stoi vs std::stol/stoll/strtol is behaviorally indistinguishable here: every value that would overflow int (>2147483647) also exceeds 65535, so both paths yield 'absent'. Likewise std::stoul cannot be ruled out: stoul("-0")==0 (accepted, matches) and stoul("-80") wraps to a huge value (>65535, rejected, also matches). Implementing as 'optional ws, optional sign, digits, accept iff 0<=signed value<=65535' reproduces all observed outputs.

Whether the range test is written as (v < 0 || v > 65535) or (v >= 0 && v <= 65535) or against an unsigned 16-bit cap is unobservable; 65535 accepted / 65536 rejected is the only boundary evidence and it is unambiguous.
has_port() could be implemented as port != -1 or port >= 0; since a successful parse can never produce a negative value, the two are indistinguishable.

isspace() is locale-dependent in principle. All six C-locale whitespace bytes are skipped; NBSP (C2 A0) is not. I could not test under a non-C locale, so a locale-sensitive difference cannot be fully excluded (the binary presumably never calls setlocale, so the classic 'C' locale set is the safe implementation).
A literal NUL byte inside the port text could not be tested (bash strips it from argv), so behavior of an embedded '\0' is unknown — likely unreachable via argv anyway.

rules.rule: The scheme delimiter is the literal 3-byte sequence "://". A scheme/authority split is attempted ONLY if that exact substring occurs; a bare ':' with one slash or no slash never triggers it. Evidence: "http:/x" and "http:x" and "a:/:/x" all yield scheme "", has_scheme 0, and the ENTIRE input as path().

There is NO character-set validation of the scheme at all. Every byte before the delimiter is accepted verbatim, including '/', ':', '@', '\\', '%', space, tab, newline, digits, leading '+', '-', '.', and non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes. Confirmed schemes: "a/b" (a/b://c), "///" (///://x), "/" (/://x), "a:b:c" (a:b:c://d), "a::" (a::://b), "1http", "ht_tp", "ht tp", "ht\ttp", "a\\b", "a@b", "a%20b", "-a", "+a", ".a", "0", "h+t-t.p", "ÄÖÜ". None of these are rejected or downgraded to path.

The ONLY thing that suppresses scheme recognition (besides the delimiter being absent) is a '?' or '#' occurring earlier in the input than the first "://". Implement as: split fragment off at the FIRST '#' of the whole input; then split query off at the FIRST '?' of the pre-fragment part; then search for "://" only in the remaining leading segment. Evidence: "ht?tp://x" -> no scheme, path "ht", query "tp://x"; "ht#tp://x" -> no scheme, path "ht", fragment "tp://x"; "?://x" -> query "://x"; "#://x" -> fragment "://x"; "a?b#c://d" -> path "a", query "b", fragment "c://d"; "a#b?c://d" -> path "a", no query, fragment "b?c://d".

When "://" does occur before any '?' or '#', the FIRST occurrence wins; later occurrences are ordinary text. Evidence: "http://a://b" -> scheme "http", host "a", path "//b"; "a://b://c://d" -> scheme "a", host "b", path "//c://d"; "AB://CD://EF" -> scheme "ab", host "CD", path "//EF".

The search is a plain substring find, so overlapping colons shift the split: in "a:://b" the first "://" starts at index 2, giving scheme "a:" and host "b". In "a:://:b" scheme is "a:" and the remainder ":b" is the authority (empty host, port "b" unparseable -> absent).

scheme() is lowercased byte-by-byte with ASCII tolower only: 'A'-'Z' -> 'a'-'z', every other byte (including UTF-8 continuation/high bytes) is left untouched. Evidence: "HTTPÄ://x" -> scheme bytes h t t p 0xC3 0x84 (verified with od -c); "HtTp://x" -> "http"; "A+B-C.D://x" -> "a+b-c.d". Host, path, query and fragment keep their original case ("Http://EXAMPLE.com/PaTh?QuEry#FrAg" -> host "EXAMPLE.com", path "/PaTh", query "QuEry", fragment "FrAg").

An input beginning with "://" yields an EMPTY scheme (has_scheme 0) but the authority IS still parsed from the text after the delimiter. Evidence: "://x" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, authority "x", host "x", has_authority 1, has_host 1; "://u@h:1/p?q#f" -> userinfo "u", host "h", port 1, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", has_scheme 0.

to_string() emits the "scheme://" + authority() prefix ONLY when has_scheme() is true. If the scheme is empty but an authority was parsed, the authority (and userinfo/host/port) is silently DROPPED from to_string(), making it lossy. Evidence: "://x" -> to_string "" (verified byte-exact empty line via od); "://x:80" -> ""; "://u@h:1/p?q#f" -> "/p?q#f"; "://a?b://c" -> "?b://c"; "://a/b?c#d" -> "/b?c#d".

Full to_string() formula consistent with every probe: (has_scheme() ? scheme() + "://" + authority() : "") + path() + (has_query() ? "?" + query() : "") + (has_fragment() ? "#" + fragment() : ""). Note authority() is the RECONSTRUCTED string and is emitted even when has_authority() is 0. Evidence: "http:////x" -> "http://"+""+"//x" = "http:////x"; "a:://:b" -> "a:"+"://"+""+"" = "a:://"; "http://:8080" -> "http://:8080" (authority ":8080" though has_authority 0); "a://?" -> "a://" (empty query delimiter dropped).

After a recognized "://", the authority runs to the first '/' in the remaining (already query/fragment-stripped) segment; that '/' and everything after it is the path. If the delimiter is immediately followed by '/', the authority is empty. Evidence: "a:///b" -> scheme a, authority "", has_authority 0, path "/b"; "http:////x" -> path "//x"; "a://///b" -> path "///b"; ":///x" -> no scheme, no authority, path "/x", to_string "/x".

Because query/fragment are split before authority parsing, '?' and '#' also terminate the authority. Evidence: "http://a#b:80" -> host "a", port -1, fragment "b:80" (NOT host "a#b" port 80); "http://a#b/c" -> host "a", path "", fragment "b/c"; "http://a?b/c" -> host "a", path "", query "b/c"; "http://a:8#0" -> port 8, fragment "0".

No whitespace is ever trimmed, at any position. Leading/trailing spaces become part of the scheme and are reproduced by to_string(). Evidence: " http://x" -> scheme " http", to_string " http://x"; "http ://x" -> scheme "http "; "a  ://x" -> scheme "a  "; " ://x" -> scheme " " (has_scheme 1!); "  ://x" -> scheme "  "; "\t://x" -> scheme "\t"; "s:// ?q" -> host " ", has_host 1, is_valid 1.

has_scheme() is exactly scheme().empty() == false. The only way to get an empty-but-present delimiter is the input starting with "://" (or the pre-query segment starting with it). A whitespace-only scheme still sets has_scheme 1.

An 'invalid-looking' scheme never causes a fallback re-parse: there is no code path that turns a bad scheme into a path. Either "://" is found in the leading segment (scheme + authority parsed, whatever the scheme text) or it is not (whole leading segment becomes path). Evidence: "a/b://c" keeps scheme "a/b" with host "c" and path ""; "a%3A%2F%2Fb" (percent-encoded) -> no scheme, path is the whole string (no percent-decoding before the search).
No length limit on the scheme was found: a 300-character 'A' run before "://" produced a 300-character lowercased scheme and round-tripped through to_string().

Side observation from these probes: is_valid() == (has_host() || has_path()). Scheme presence is irrelevant to validity. Evidence: "a://" -> 0; "abc://" -> 0; "://:8080" -> 0 (port only); "?://x" -> 0 (query only); "#://x" -> 0 (fragment only); "http://?q" -> 0; "://x" -> 1 (host only); ":///x" -> 1 (path only); "s:// ?q" -> 1 (host is a single space).

A newline inside argv ends up inside the scheme, so the program then prints MORE than 18 physical lines (the scheme field itself spans two lines). Evidence: $'ht
tp://x' -> scheme "ht
tp". Any consumer that assumes exactly 18 lines must treat fields as 
-delimited-with-embedded-newlines only if it knows the input.

rules.rule: THE PREDICATE: is_valid() == ( !host().empty() || !path().empty() ). Equivalently: is_valid() == (has_host() || has_path()). Nothing else in the parse result influences it. Pseudocode: bool is_valid() const { return !host_.empty() || !path_.empty(); }

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of scheme presence. 'http:///p' -> scheme 'http', host '', path '/p' -> valid 1. '/just/a/path' -> no scheme, path non-empty -> valid 1. 'http://' -> scheme 'http', host '', path '' -> valid 0. There is no 'scheme implies host' requirement.

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of the scheme's identity and charset — there is NO known-scheme whitelist. With a non-empty host all of these are valid 1: http, https, ftp, file, ws, mailto, data, 'zzz', 'q', 'x1', 'HTTP', 'Http', 'a-b', 'a+b', 'a.b', '1', '9z', '1abc', 'a b' (with a space), '%' , ' ' (scheme is literally one space). With an empty host and empty path all of the same schemes give valid 0. Scheme charset/length/case is never validated.
is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of query(). 'http://:80?q' -> host '', path '', query 'q' -> valid 0. '?a=b' -> query 'a=b' -> valid 0. A non-empty query can never rescue an otherwise-invalid URL.
is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of fragment(). '#f' -> fragment 'f' -> valid 0. 'http://:80#f' -> fragment 'f', host '', path '' -> valid 0. 'http://u@#f' -> userinfo 'u', fragment 'f' -> valid 0.

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of userinfo(). 'http://u@' -> userinfo 'u', host '', path '' -> valid 0. 'http://u:p@' -> valid 0. 'http://u@/p' -> userinfo 'u', host '', path '/p' -> valid 1 (the path, not the userinfo, makes it valid).

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of port(). 'http://:8080' -> port 8080, host '', path '' -> valid 0. 'http://:80/p' -> port 80, host '', path '/p' -> valid 1. 'http://h:65536' and 'http://h:99999' and 'http://h:-1' -> port absent (-1) but host 'h' -> valid 1. An out-of-range/unparseable port never invalidates.

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of to_string(). Counterexamples both ways: '://x' -> to_string '' (empty!) yet valid 1; '?a=b' -> to_string '?a=b' (non-empty) yet valid 0; 'http://u@' -> to_string 'http://u@' yet valid 0. Do not implement is_valid via to_string.

Whitespace and control bytes count as ordinary non-empty content. ' ' (one space) -> path ' ' -> valid 1. '  ' -> valid 1. tab -> path tab -> valid 1. 'a\nb' -> path 'a', query 'b' -> valid 1. 0x01 -> path 0x01 -> valid 1. 'http:// ' -> host ' ' (a single space), has_host 1 -> valid 1. 'http://  ' -> host '  ' -> valid 1. There is NO trimming and no whitespace rejection.
Empty input is the only length-0 case: '' -> all fields empty -> valid 0.

Inputs that reduce to pure delimiters with no host and no path are invalid: '?' -> 0, '#' -> 0, '??' -> 0, '?#' -> 0, '#?' -> 0, '###' -> 0, '??q' -> 0, '://' -> 0, '://:80' -> 0, '://u@' -> 0, 'http://?' -> 0, 'http://#' -> 0, 'http://?#' -> 0, 'ZZZ://' -> 0. In every one of these both host and path are empty.

Any single character other than '?' and '#' is valid, because it lands in path: 'a' -> 1, '0' -> 1, '-' -> 1, '.' -> 1, '/' -> 1, ':' -> path ':' -> 1, '%' -> 1, ' ' -> 1, tab -> 1. Only '?' and '#' are consumed as delimiters and leave path empty.

When '://' is present the authority is parsed even if the scheme part is EMPTY, and that parsed host makes the URL valid with has_scheme 0: '://x' -> scheme '' (has_scheme 0), host 'x', valid 1. '://h:80' -> host 'h', valid 1. ' ://h' -> scheme ' ' (has_scheme 1), host 'h', valid 1.

has_authority() == !host().empty() — it matched exactly in all ~7000 probes, including 'http://:8080' (authority ':8080', has_authority 0), 'http://u@' (authority 'u@', has_authority 0), and 'http:// ' (host ' ', has_authority 1). So has_authority() is exactly has_host().
is_valid() never depends on input length or byte values: a 300-char host -> 1; a 200-char all-'/' path -> 1; non-UTF8 bytes 0xFF 0xFE as path -> 1; 'café' as path or host -> 1.

Process behavior: with argc >= 2 the binary always prints exactly 18 lines and exits 0, including for invalid URLs ('' , '?' -> exit 0). With argc < 2 it prints nothing and exits 1. is_valid being 0 does NOT change the exit code or suppress output.

rules.rule:
The authority segment emitted by to_string() is byte-identical to authority(), i.e. rebuilt from the three sub-parts, NOT the raw input substring:
  authority() = (userinfo_.empty() ? "" : userinfo_ + "@") + host_ + (port_ == -1 ? "" : ":" + std::to_string(port_))
Every probe had to_string()'s authority slice == the printed authority() field, including the degenerate ones ('http://:8080' -> ':8080', 'http://u@' -> 'u@', 'http://u@:99/p' -> 'u@:99').

Q1 ANSWER: "://" is emitted whenever scheme_ is non-empty, unconditionally — it does NOT depend on the authority being present or non-empty. 'http://' (empty authority, has_authority 0) round-trips exactly to 'http://'. 'http://:/' -> 'http:///' (scheme + "://" + empty authority + path "/"), producing three consecutive slashes.

Q5 ANSWER: to_string() NEVER emits "//" without a scheme. The authority is emitted only inside the `if (!scheme_.empty())` branch, so when a parsed authority exists but the scheme is empty it is SILENTLY DISCARDED. This is the most surprising/most destructive lossy case: '://h' -> to_string "" (empty!) even though host()=='h' and has_host()==1; '://h/p' -> '/p'; '://h?q#f' -> '?q#f'; '://a' -> ''. The gate is the emptiness of the scheme STRING, not whether the "://" delimiter was found.

The scheme gate is `!scheme_.empty()`, not "delimiter was found" and not any character-class validity test. A scheme of a single space qualifies: ' ://h' round-trips exactly to ' ://h' (scheme==" ", so " " + "://" + "h" is emitted).

Q2 ANSWER: '?' is emitted if and only if query_ is non-empty; '#' is emitted if and only if fragment_ is non-empty. Delimiters present in the input with empty content are therefore dropped: 'http://h/?' -> 'http://h/', 'http://h/#' -> 'http://h/', 'http://h/p?#' -> 'http://h/p', 'http://h?q#' -> 'http://h?q', 'http://h?#f' -> 'http://h#f', '?' -> '', '#' -> '', '?#' -> '', '?#f' -> '#f'. A query/fragment consisting of a delimiter character IS non-empty and is preserved: 'http://h/??' -> 'http://h/??' (query=="?"), 'http://h/##' -> 'http://h/##' (fragment=="#"), 'http://h/#?' -> 'http://h/#?'.

path_ is appended unconditionally and verbatim, with no separator logic at all. No '/' is inserted between authority and query/fragment when path is empty: 'http://h?q' -> 'http://h?q', 'http://h#f' -> 'http://h#f'. Conversely a path is emitted with no scheme/authority prefix: '/p' -> '/p', '//example.com/path' -> '//example.com/path' (the whole thing is path).

Order of emitted pieces is fixed: scheme, "://", userinfo, "@", host, ":", port, path, "?", query, "#", fragment. Confirmed by the full-house probe 'http://user:pw@host:8080/p/q?a=b#frag' -> identical output.

LOSSY CLASS 1 - scheme case folding. The scheme is lowercased with byte-wise C-locale tolower (ASCII A-Z only; non-ASCII bytes untouched). 'HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM' -> 'http://EXAMPLE.COM'; 'HTTP://U@H:80/P?Q#F' -> 'http://U@H:80/P?Q#F' (only the scheme is folded, userinfo/host/path/query/fragment keep their case). Non-ASCII proof: 'ÜNÏ://h' -> 'ÜnÏ://h' — raw bytes 303 234 'n' 303 217, i.e. only the ASCII 'N' changed while the UTF-8 continuation bytes 0xEA/0xCC passed through unmodified.

LOSSY CLASS 2 - empty scheme with '://' present: the entire authority AND the '://' vanish (see the Q5 rule). Inputs: '://' -> '', '://h' -> '', '://a' -> '', '://h#f' -> '#f', '://h/p?q#f' -> '/p?q#f'.
LOSSY CLASS 3 - empty query and/or empty fragment delimiters are dropped (see Q2 rule).

LOSSY CLASS 4 - an '@' with empty userinfo is dropped, because authority() only emits '@' when userinfo is non-empty: 'http://@h' -> 'http://h'; 'http://@' -> 'http://'. Note a userinfo of just ':' is non-empty and survives: 'http://:@h' -> 'http://:@h'. With multiple '@', userinfo is the part before the FIRST '@' and the rest stays in host, so it still round-trips: 'http://a@b@h/p' -> 'http://a@b@h/p' (userinfo 'a', host 'b@h').

LOSSY CLASS 5 - port canonicalization to decimal via std::to_string(port). Any non-canonical spelling is rewritten: 'http://h:065' -> 'http://h:65'; 'http://h:00080' -> 'http://h:80'; 'http://h:+80/p' -> 'http://h:80/p'; 'http://h: 80/p' -> 'http://h:80/p'; 'http://h:-0' -> 'http://h:0' (accepted, port 0!); 'http://h:0080abc/p?q#f' -> 'http://h:80/p?q#f' (trailing garbage stripped). Canonical values are stable: 'http://h:0', 'http://h:80', 'http://h:65535' all round-trip exactly.

LOSSY CLASS 6 - rejected port: when the port fails to parse or is out of range, the whole ':<portstring>' is deleted from the output (the ':' goes too). 'http://h:abc' -> 'http://h'; 'http://u@h:abc/p' -> 'http://u@h/p'; 'http://h:65536/p' -> 'http://h/p'; 'http://h:2147483647' -> 'http://h' (INT_MAX parses fine via stoi but fails the range check, so the accepted range is 0..65535 inclusive); 'http://u@h:99999999999999/p' -> 'http://u@h/p'; 'http://h:' -> 'http://' (host also empty here).
LOSSY CLASS 7 - empty port after ':': 'http://:' -> 'http://', 'http://h:' -> 'http://h' (established fact re-confirmed via authority reconstruction).

LOSSY CLASS 8 - host/port split happens at the FIRST ':' in the post-userinfo authority, so anything after a second ':' is destroyed. 'http://a:b:80' -> 'http://a' (host 'a', port rejected from 'b:80'); 'http://h:80:90' -> 'http://h:80' (port stoi("80:90")==80, ':90' dropped).
LOSSY CLASS 9 - IPv6 literals are mangled, a direct consequence of class 8: 'http://[::1]:80/p' -> 'http://[/p'. host()=='[' , port absent. There is no bracket handling whatsoever.

Q4 ANSWER - ROUND-TRIP IDENTITY CONDITION. to_string(input) == input if and only if ALL of the following hold:
 1. Either the input contains no usable "://", or the substring before the first usable "://" is non-empty and contains no ASCII uppercase letter.
 2. If an '@' appears in the authority, the text before the first '@' is non-empty.
 3. If a ':' appears in the post-userinfo authority, the text after it up to the authority terminator is the exact canonical decimal form of an integer in [0, 65535] (no sign, no leading zeros except the single digit "0", no leading spaces, no trailing characters, and no further ':').
 4. If a '?' query delimiter is consumed, the query is non-empty; if a '#' fragment delimiter is consumed, the fragment is non-empty.
Otherwise the output is shorter/different per lossy classes 1-9. Measured rate: 46,592 of 51,200 structured combinations in a sweep over scheme/userinfo/host/port/path/query/fragment variants were lossy.

to_string() is IDEMPOTENT as a string function: to_string(to_string(x)) == to_string(x) for all 2,599 corpus inputs tested, 0 violations. It is NOT information-preserving, though — '://h/p' -> '/p' is a fixed point but the second parse has host()=='' where the first had host()=='h'.

Bytes are copied raw with no encoding or escaping. TAB survives in path, query and fragment ('http://h/a\tb?q\tx#f\ty' round-trips byte-for-byte). CR survives in host ('http://h\r/p' -> 'http://h\r/p'). An embedded LF in the path is emitted literally, which makes the program print 20 newline-terminated lines instead of 18 — any harness that assumes exactly 18 lines will desynchronize on inputs containing '\n'. Leading/trailing spaces are preserved (' http://h/p' -> scheme ' http', round-trips; 'http://h/p ' -> path '/p ', round-trips; 'http://h /p' -> host 'h ', round-trips).

to_string() ignores has_authority()/has_host()/has_userinfo()/has_path()/has_query()/has_fragment() as gates; the only flag-like test it makes is the implicit port_ != -1 inside authority(). Proof that has_authority() is not consulted: 'http://:8080' has has_authority()==0 yet to_string()=='http://:8080'. Proof that has_host() is not consulted: 'http://h' with has_host()==1 vs '://h' with has_host()==1 give 'http://h' and '' respectively — only the scheme differs.

to_string() output is unrelated to is_valid(): invalid URLs still serialize ('http://' -> 'http://' with is_valid 0; 'http://u:p@:99' -> 'http://u:p@:99' with is_valid 0; '?q' -> '?q' with is_valid 0), and to_string() can be empty for a valid URL ('://h' -> '' with is_valid 1).

Scheme detection (relevant because it gates the whole authority segment): the '#' and '?' splits happen before scheme recognition, so a '#' or '?' preceding the "://" suppresses the scheme and thus the authority. 'ht#tp://h' -> no scheme, path 'ht', fragment 'tp://h', round-trips. 'ht?tp://h' -> no scheme, path 'ht', query 'tp://h', round-trips. 'a?b://c' -> path 'a', query 'b://c'. 'MAILTO:x@y' -> no scheme (no "://"), path 'MAILTO:x@y', round-trips (note: NOT lowercased, confirming lowercasing applies only to the scheme field). By contrast '/' and ':' inside the scheme candidate are allowed: '/a://b' -> scheme '/a', round-trips; 'a/b://c' -> scheme 'a/b'; 'a b://c' -> scheme 'a b'; ':://a' -> scheme ':'. Only the FIRST "://" counts: 'http://h/a://b' -> scheme 'http', path '/a://b', round-trips.

Whether to_string() literally calls authority() or re-derives userinfo/host/port inline is not observable from the outside: every probe produced a to_string authority slice byte-identical to the printed authority() field, including all degenerate combinations. Implementing it either way is safe.

Whether the scheme gate is `!scheme_.empty()` or a separate boolean `has_scheme_` member is not distinguishable, because I found no input where the scheme string is empty but a scheme was 'found' in a way that produced any output difference — '://x' consistently emits nothing for the scheme+authority portion. Both implementations behave identically on everything I probed.

Port acceptance boundary: I confirmed 0, 65534 and 65535 accepted and 65536, 2147483647, 99999999999999 and -80 rejected, so the check is almost certainly 0 <= p <= 65535. I did not probe every value in between, and I did not determine whether the rejection of huge values comes from a std::out_of_range catch or from the explicit range check (both end in the same observable behavior: the whole ':port' is omitted).

'-0' being accepted as port 0 (emitted as ':0') while '-80' is rejected is genuinely surprising and worth a dedicated regression test; it implies the sign is consumed by the integer parse and only the resulting VALUE is range-checked, rather than the port string being screened for a leading '-'.

Exact ordering of scheme-detection vs the '#'/'?' splits: my evidence ('ht#tp://h', 'ht?tp://h', 'a?b://c' all yield no scheme, while '/a://b', 'a/b://c', 'a b://c', ':://a' all yield a scheme) is equally consistent with (a) splitting fragment then query first and only then searching the remainder for '://', or (b) searching for '://' first and rejecting the candidate if it contains '#' or '?'. I could not construct an input that separates the two models. This matters for to_string only because it decides whether the authority is emitted at all.

Inputs containing a literal LF break the '18 lines of output' contract: to_string() re-emits the newline verbatim, so 'http://h/a\nb' prints 20 lines. Any differential-testing harness must compare raw bytes or split on a known field count rather than assuming 18 lines.

to_string() is idempotent as a string transform (0 violations in 2,599 tries) but is NOT information-preserving: for '://h' the first parse has host()=='h' while the reparse of its to_string ('') has no host. So to_string cannot be used as a canonical key for parse-equivalence.

PARSE ORDER (this is the key structural rule, and it differs from the 'split after authority' description): (1) fragment = everything after the FIRST '#' in the WHOLE input; rest = prefix before it. (2) query = everything after the FIRST '?' in `rest`; rest2 = prefix before it. (3) In rest2 only, search for the FIRST occurrence of the literal "://": if found at index i, scheme = rest2[0..i) (lowercased), and authority region starts at i+3; otherwise the whole rest2 is the path. Because '#'/'?' are removed first, a "://" that occurs after a '?' or '#' is NEVER treated as a scheme separator: "a?b://c" -> scheme "", path "a", query "b://c"; "#x://h" -> fragment "x://h", path "".

Authority region ends at the FIRST of '/', '?' or '#' — but since '?'/'#' were already stripped in steps 1-2, in practice it ends at the first '/' or at end of rest2. Everything from that '/' onward (inside rest2) is the path. "a://b://c" -> scheme a, host b, path "//c"; "http://h?q@x/p" -> authority "h", query "q@x/p".

Within the authority region: userinfo = text before the FIRST '@' (last '@' is NOT used): "http://a@b@c:80/p" -> userinfo "a", host "b@c", port 80. Then in the remainder, host = text before the FIRST ':' and port-token = text after it (later colons stay in the port token and are simply where stoi stops): "http://h:1:2/p" -> host "h", port 1. "http://u:p:q@h/p" -> userinfo "u:p:q", host "h".

NO IPv6 bracket support at all. "http://[::1]:8080/p" -> host "[", port -1 (stoi("::1]:8080") fails), authority "[", to_string "http://[/p" — i.e. the URL is silently corrupted and is_valid is still 1. Same for "http://[::1]/p".

NO trimming of any whitespace anywhere. Leading/trailing spaces are kept and become part of scheme and/or path: "  http://h/p  " -> scheme "  http" (has_scheme 1), path "/p  ", to_string "  http://h/p  ". An input of only spaces becomes the path (" " -> path " ", has_path 1, is_valid 1). Host may be pure whitespace: "http://   /p" -> host "   ", has_host 1.

Every byte other than the structural delimiters passes through completely untouched: tab, CR, LF, DEL(0x7f), control bytes 0x01-0x04, raw high bytes 0x80/0xFF, valid UTF-8 (U+00E4 = C3 A4), a UTF-8 BOM (EF BB BF), and invalid UTF-8. Verified byte-for-byte with od -c in scheme, host, path, query and fragment. No percent-decoding, no percent-validation, no encoding, no normalization: "%", "%zz", "%4", "%25" all survive verbatim in host/path/query/fragment, and '%' is even a legal scheme ("%://h" -> scheme "%", host "h").

scheme() lowercasing is ASCII-only, byte-wise (equivalent to tolower() in the C locale): 'A'-'Z' -> 'a'-'z'; bytes >= 0x80 are untouched. "htTPÜ://…" -> scheme "httpÜ" (C3 9C preserved); input "AAA\xC0\xDE://h/p" -> scheme "aaa\xC0\xDE". Non-alphabetic ASCII is unchanged. host()/path()/query()/fragment() case is never changed.

The scheme is an unconstrained byte string: it may contain spaces, tabs, '/', '%', high bytes, anything, as long as it appears before the first "://" and after the '?'/'#' stripping. "a/b://c" -> scheme "a/b", host "c"; "a b://c/d" -> scheme "a b"; " ://h/p" -> scheme " " (has_scheme 1) and to_string " ://h/p".

An input beginning with "://" yields an EMPTY scheme (has_scheme 0) but the authority IS still parsed: "://h/p" -> host "h", has_host 1, has_authority 1, path "/p". Special case: "://" alone produces output byte-identical to the empty input (all fields empty, port -1, all flags 0, to_string "", is_valid 0).

to_string() = (has_scheme() ? scheme + "://" + authority() : "") + path + (has_query() ? "?" + query : "") + (has_fragment() ? "#" + fragment : ""). Consequences: (a) when scheme is empty the authority is DROPPED from to_string even though has_authority may be 1 — "://h:80/p" -> to_string "/p" (lossy); (b) the authority part is emitted whenever has_scheme, regardless of has_authority — "http://u@:80/p" -> to_string "http://u@:80/p", "http://@/p" -> to_string "http:///p"; (c) empty query/fragment markers are dropped — "http://h/p?#" -> to_string "http://h/p".

authority() is rebuilt as (userinfo.empty()? "" : userinfo + "@") + host + (port==-1 ? "" : ":" + to_string(port)). An empty userinfo before '@' is dropped ("://@h" -> authority "h"); a non-numeric port token is dropped ("http://h:\"80\"/p" -> authority "h"); a truncated stoi result is re-serialized ("http://h:0x10/p" -> authority "h:0", "http://h:1:2/p" -> authority "h:1").

has_authority() == !host.empty() (i.e. it is exactly has_host()), NOT 'authority string non-empty'. Evidence: "://:80" -> authority ":80" but has_authority 0; "http://u@:80/p" -> authority "u@:80", has_userinfo 1, has_port 1, has_authority 0; "http://u@" -> authority "u@", has_authority 0. Across ~120 probes has_authority never differed from has_host.

has_scheme/has_userinfo/has_host/has_path/has_query/has_fragment are all exactly 'field string is non-empty' (a single space counts as non-empty: "http://h/p? # " -> query " " has_query 1, fragment " " has_fragment 1). has_port() == (port != -1), and port 0 counts as present ("http://:0" -> port 0, has_port 1).

is_valid() == (!host.empty() || !path.empty()), i.e. has_host() || has_path(). Nothing else matters — scheme, userinfo, port, query and fragment are all irrelevant. Evidence: "#f"->0, "?q"->0, "#?"->0, "a://"->0, "a://?q"->0, "a://#f"->0, "http://u@"->0, "http://u@?q"->0 (userinfo present), "http://:0"->0 (port present), ""->0, "://"->0; versus " "->1 (path " "), "@"->1 (path "@"), "http://h"->1 (host only), "http:///p"->1 (path only), "://h"->1.

Port token parsing is std::stoi + range check on the token after the first ':' in the host part: leading whitespace (space, tab, \v, \f, \r — all verified) and a leading '+' are skipped, digits are consumed greedily and parsing stops at the first non-digit, so "80abc"/"80 "/"0x10"/"1e3"/"8_0"/"8 0" -> 80/80/0/1/8/8; no leading digit after optional sign/space ("", "abc", '"80"', "::1]…") -> absent (-1); values > INT_MAX or negative ("-80", "65536", 100 nines) -> absent (-1). Absent port prints -1, has_port 0, and is omitted from authority() and to_string().

Repeated delimiters: only the first of each matters and the rest are literal data. "http://h/p??q?r" -> query "?q?r"; "http://h/p#a#b#c" -> fragment "a#b#c"; "http://h#f?q" -> fragment "f?q" and NO query; 1000 consecutive ':' after the host -> host "h", port -1; 1000 consecutive '@' -> userinfo "u", host = the remaining 999 '@' + "h" (length 1000).

Size: no internal length limit observed. A 120,016-byte URL (host 10,000 chars, path 100,000 chars, query 5,002, fragment 5,000, port 8080) parses with exact field contents and a byte-exact 120,016-char to_string round-trip. Inputs up to 131,070 bytes work; 131,072+ fails with execve 'Argument list too long' (rc 126 from the shell) — that is the Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN limit (128 KiB per argument), not a program limit. No crash, no truncation, no quadratic slowdown noticed.
Option-looking arguments get no special treatment: "-h" -> path "-h", is_valid 1; "--help" -> path "--help". There is no flag parsing and no usage message on stdout for any argc >= 2.

Bare '@' or ':' or '//' with no "://" are plain path text: "@"->path "@"; ":"->path ":"; ":/"->path ":/"; "//"->path "//"; "://://"->scheme "" + path "//"; "http://://h" -> scheme http, authority empty, path "//h", to_string "http:////h".

to_string() is lossy/asymmetric in three ways that look like bugs rather than design: (a) when the scheme is empty but '://' was present, the authority is silently dropped ("://h:80/p" -> "/p"), so to_string is not a round-trip; (b) when has_scheme is true the authority is emitted even when has_authority() is false ("http://u@:80/p"); (c) '?' / '#' with empty content are dropped. The 131072-byte failure is an OS execve limit (MAX_ARG_STRLEN), so I could not determine whether the library has any internal size limit above 128 KiB. No limit was observed up to 131070 bytes.

I did not manage to distinguish 'authority ends at first of /?#' from 'authority ends at first /' because '?' and '#' are already removed before the authority is parsed; both models predict every observed output. Implementing either is safe.
NUL bytes cannot be passed through argv, so behavior on embedded NUL is untestable and unknown.

result.family: Systematic structural combination sweep (scheme x userinfo x host x port x path x query x fragment cartesian products)

rules.rule:
COMPLETE ALGORITHM (validated byte-for-byte on 6,900+ inputs against the binary with ZERO mismatches; implement exactly this):
  rest = input; scheme=""; ui=""; host=""; port=-1; path=""; query=""; frag=""; parse_authority=false
  k = rest.find("://")                      // FIRST occurrence only
  if k != npos: scheme = tolower(rest[0..k)); rest = rest[k+3..]; parse_authority = true
  h = rest.find('#'); if h != npos: frag = rest[h+1..]; rest = rest[0..h)
  q = rest.find('?'); if q != npos: query = rest[q+1..]; rest = rest[0..q)
  if parse_authority:
      s = rest.find('/')
      if s != npos: a = rest[0..s); path = rest[s..]   else: a = rest; path = ""
      at = a.find('@'); if at != npos: ui = a[0..at); a = a[at+1..]
      c  = a.find(':')
      if c != npos: host = a[0..c); v = try_stoi(a[c+1..]); port = (v ok && 0<=v<=65535) ? v : -1
      else: host = a
  else: path = rest
  authority = (ui.empty()? "" : ui+"@") + host + (port!=-1 ? ":"+itoa(port) : "")
  to_string = (scheme.empty()? "" : scheme+"://"+authority) + path + (query.empty()?"":"?"+query) + (frag.empty()?"":"#"+frag)
  has_X = !X.empty() for scheme/userinfo/host/path/query/fragment; has_port = (port != -1); has_authority = !host.empty()
  is_valid = !host.empty() || !path.empty()

has_authority() == has_host() == (host string non-empty). It is NOT 'authority string non-empty' and NOT 'authority was parsed'. Identical on all 6,900 probes: "http://:8080" -> authority ":8080" but has_authority 0; "http://u@" -> authority "u@" but has_authority 0; "http://h.com@/p" -> authority "h.com@", host "", has_authority 0.

is_valid() == (has_host() || has_path()). Nothing else matters - scheme, port, query, fragment are all irrelevant. Evidence: "http://:80"->0 (port only), "http://:80/p"->1, "http://?a=1"->0, "http://#f"->0, "?a=1"->0, "#f"->0, "/"->1, "http:///p"->1, "http://u@"->0, "http://u@/p"->1, ""->0, "http://"->0, "://h.com"->1.

Scheme detection uses the FIRST occurrence of the literal "://" and takes EVERYTHING before it as the scheme, with no character-class validation whatsoever. "http:://h.com" -> scheme "http:"; "a:b://h.com" -> scheme "a:b"; "1://h.com" -> scheme "1"; " http://h.com" -> scheme " http"; "http+s://h.com" -> scheme "http+s"; "h-t.p://h.com" -> scheme "h-t.p". No "://" anywhere => no scheme AND no authority parsing at all ("http:/h.com" -> path is the whole string).

SURPRISING/decoupled: finding "://" enables authority parsing even when the scheme is EMPTY. "://h.com" -> scheme "", has_scheme 0, but host "h.com", authority "h.com", has_authority 1, is_valid 1. Authority parsing is gated on 'saw \"://\"'; has_scheme is gated on 'scheme non-empty'. Two independent conditions.

SURPRISING/lossy: to_string() emits the scheme+authority block ONLY when the scheme is non-empty, so with an empty scheme the whole authority is silently dropped. "://h.com" -> to_string "" (empty string!); "://u@h.com:80/p?a=1#f" -> to_string "/p?a=1#f"; "://:80/p" -> to_string "/p". This is the only case where to_string loses entire components.

Only the FIRST "://" is consumed; later "://" stays in the remainder and is treated structurally. "http://x://y" -> authority raw "x:", host "x", port -1 (stoi("") fails), path "//y", to_string "http://x//y". "x://y://z/p" -> scheme "x", host "y", path "//z/p". "http://h.com://x" -> host "h.com", path "//x".

Splitting order: scheme first, then fragment (first '#' in the remainder), then query (first '?' in the part before that '#'), then the authority/path split. Consequence: '?' and '#' terminate the authority even with no '/'. "http://h.com?a=1" -> host "h.com", path "", query "a=1". "http://h.co#m:80/p" -> host "h.co", fragment "m:80/p" (":80" is NOT a port). "http://h.co?m:80/p" -> host "h.co", query "m:80/p". "http://h.com?a=1/b" -> query "a=1/b", path "".

path = everything from the FIRST '/' in the post-scheme, post-fragment, post-query remainder, inclusive, to its end; if that remainder has no '/', path is empty. Path is verbatim: no normalization ("/a/./b/../c" preserved), no percent-decoding, and '@'/':' inside it are inert ("http://h.com/p@q" -> path "/p@q"; "http://h.com/p:80" -> path "/p:80", port -1).

userinfo is split at the FIRST '@' in the authority substring, not the last. "http://a@b@h.com/p" -> userinfo "a", host "b@h.com", has_host 1. "http://a@b@c.com:80/p" -> userinfo "a", host "b@c.com", port 80. So a host may legitimately contain '@'.

host is split at the FIRST ':' after userinfo removal; everything after that ':' is the port string (which may itself contain ':'). "http://h.com:80:90" -> host "h.com", port 80 (stoi stops at ':'), to_string "http://h.com:80". "http://h.com::80" -> host "h.com", portstr ":80", stoi fails, port -1. "http://a:b:c@h.com:80" -> userinfo "a:b:c" ('@' split runs first), host "h.com", port 80.

SURPRISING: IPv6 bracket literals are completely unsupported and DATA IS LOST. "http://[::1]" -> host "[" (the bare bracket), port -1, authority "[", to_string "http://[" - "::1]" vanishes entirely (neither host, port, nor path). "http://[::1]:80/p" -> host "[", path "/p", to_string "http://[/p". "http://[2001:db8::1]/p" -> host "[2001", path "/p", to_string "http://[2001/p". Cause: first-':' split makes portstr ":1]" / "db8::1]", stoi rejects it, and the rejected text is never re-attached.

An empty userinfo before '@' is indistinguishable from no '@': "http://@h.com/p" -> userinfo "", has_userinfo 0, authority "h.com", to_string "http://h.com/p" ('@' dropped). Conversely "http://h.com@/p" -> userinfo "h.com", host "", authority "h.com@", has_authority 0, to_string "http://h.com@/p".

Port acceptance is exactly: std::stoi(portstr) (skip leading whitespace, optional +/-, then digits, stopping at the first non-digit; throw on no-digits or overflow) then require 0 <= v <= 65535, else port = -1. Confirmed: ":65535"->65535, ":65536"->-1, ":2147483647"->-1, ":2147483648"->-1, ":9999999999999999999999"->-1, ":0"->0, ":-1"->-1, ":065"->65, ":+80"->80, ":  +65535xyz"->65535, ":80abc"->80, ":"->-1, ":abc"->-1.

authority() is ALWAYS the reconstruction (ui.empty()?"":ui+"@") + host + (port!=-1?":"+itoa(port):"") - verified on every one of the 6,900 probes. A rejected port therefore disappears from authority() ("http://h.com:abc" -> authority "h.com") and an accepted port is re-serialized canonically ("http://h.com:065" -> authority "h.com:65").

to_string() == input for the large majority of structurally-normal inputs. In the assigned 631-probe sweep, to_string() differed in exactly 340 cases, and EVERY difference has one of four causes: (1) scheme contained uppercase (lowercased) - 139 cases, all the ZZZ:// arm; (2) port string unparseable or outside [0,65535] (dropped together with its ':') - 96 cases (:99999 and :abc arms); (3) host was a bracketed IPv6 literal (truncated at '[') - 45 cases; (4) input had an EMPTY query (standalone/trailing '?') or EMPTY fragment (standalone/trailing '#'), dropped with its delimiter - 156 cases. Two further causes appear outside that sweep: (5) empty scheme with "://" present drops the whole authority; (6) an empty userinfo's '@' is dropped.

Empty query and empty fragment are indistinguishable from absent, and their delimiters are not preserved: "http://h.com?" -> query "", has_query 0, to_string "http://h.com"; "http://h.com#" -> to_string "http://h.com"; "http://h.com/p?#f" -> query "", fragment "f", to_string "http://h.com/p#f" ('?' lost); "?" -> to_string ""; "#" -> to_string ""; "?#" -> to_string "".

Only the scheme is case-folded (ASCII tolower). userinfo, host, path, query, fragment preserve case exactly: "HTTP://H.COM:80/P?A=1#F" -> scheme "http", host "H.COM", path "/P", query "A=1", fragment "F", to_string "http://H.COM:80/P?A=1#F". "Http://h.com" and "hTTp://h.com" both -> scheme "http". Scheme names are never special-cased: "ZZZ://", "ftp://", "https://" behave identically to "http://" (no default ports, no scheme-specific validation).

With no "://" present, ALL of authority/userinfo/host/port stay empty no matter how authority-like the input looks, and the entire input becomes path (minus the fragment/query split). "u:p@h.com:80/p" -> path "u:p@h.com:80/p", host "", port -1, is_valid 1. ":80" -> path ":80". "//" -> path "//". "h.com:99999/p" -> path "h.com:99999/p". "u@[::1]:abc" -> path "u@[::1]:abc" (IPv6 survives intact here, unlike with a scheme).

No whitespace trimming and no character rejection anywhere: raw spaces/tabs survive in every component. "http://h.com " -> host "h.com " (trailing space), to_string == input. "http://h co.com/p" -> host "h co.com". " http://h.com" -> scheme " http", has_scheme 1, to_string == input.

Path/query/fragment parsing is fully orthogonal to scheme/userinfo/host/port. Across the full 4x4x4 path x query x fragment product, the path/query/fragment/has_path/has_query/has_fragment lines were byte-identical for prefixes "", "http://h.com", "http://u:p@h.com:80", "://", and "ZZZ://h.com:abc". The only cross-effect is that a missing "://" forces path to absorb the authority text.

Fragment retains all later '#' and '?' characters; query retains all later '?' and '/' characters; path retains ':' and '@'. "http://h.com#f?g" -> fragment "f?g"; "http://h.com#f/b" -> fragment "f/b"; "http://h.com?a=1#f/b" -> query "a=1", fragment "f/b"; "http://h.com/p?a=1:2" -> query "a=1:2"; "http://h.com/p#f:2" -> fragment "f:2".

An empty authority with a scheme is legal and round-trips: "http:///p" -> host "", path "/p", has_authority 0, is_valid 1, to_string "http:///p". "http://////" -> authority "", path "////", to_string "http://////" (authority ends at the '/' found at offset 0).

ambiguities: has_authority() is observationally identical to has_host() on all 6,900 probes, so I cannot distinguish 'has_authority == !host.empty()' from 'has_authority == (saw "://" && !host.empty())'. Both models fit every observation, because host can only be non-empty when "://" was found. Either is safe to implement.
Likewise is_valid() == (has_host() || has_path()) is indistinguishable from (has_authority() || has_path()) for the same reason. No probe separates them.

Port rejection cannot be attributed to a specific mechanism: a std::stoi std::out_of_range throw (":9999999999999999999999", ":2147483648") and an explicit post-parse range check (":65536") produce identical output (port -1, dropped from authority() and to_string()). ":-80"/":-1" likewise cannot distinguish 'negative rejected by range check' from 'sign not accepted'.

The relative order of the authority/path split versus the query/fragment split is not observable: 'strip fragment, strip query, then find the first / in the remainder' and 'end authority at the first of / ? #' are provably equivalent on all inputs and both matched every probe. I chose the former in the stated algorithm.

The to_string() behavior for an empty scheme ("://h.com" -> to_string "") looks like an unintentional bug rather than a designed rule, but it is 100% reproducible across the whole "://" arm of the sweep. Any reimplementation judged byte-for-byte against the binary MUST replicate it.

std::stoi's whitespace skipping was probed only with ASCII spaces (":  +65535xyz"); I did not probe a tab/\v/\f immediately after the ':' in a port, so locale/isspace details there are inferred rather than observed.

Multi-byte UTF-8 was probed only inside a path ("http://h.com/unicode-bytes", matched the byte-level model); I did not probe multi-byte bytes as a scheme or inside a port. Byte-level (not codepoint-level) handling is assumed.
Inputs containing a NUL byte are unreachable through argv, so behavior on embedded NUL is untestable via this harness.
